title: Continuous batching scheduler tuning experiments 4
content:
Purpose:
Run microbenchmarks and production-like canary tests to understand how continuous batching scheduler knobs (batch_size cap, max_wait_ms/timeout, fairness policy) affect throughput, cost, and tail latency under realistic request mixes. This doc summarizes experiments 4 (follow-ups on earlier runs) and proposes a safe rollout plan.

Background/context:
- Continuous batching is our primary latency/cost optimization: it aggregates short generation requests into larger micro-batches to increase GPU utilization.
- Key knobs: max_batch_size (per-GPU), max_wait_ms (how long scheduler waits to fill batch), fairness policy (FIFO, StrictFair, Priority), and per-tenant shaping.
- Observed tension: larger batches => better token/sec but higher P99 for short requests. Timeouts control this trade-off. Fairness policies can reduce tenant tail latency but may reduce overall throughput.

Goals for this experiment run:
1) Quantify P50/P95/P99 and throughput for combinations of batch_size and max_wait_ms on two workload mixes (interactive short requests and long-generative requests).
2) Measure fairness policy impact on tail latency for multi-tenant hot-spot scenarios.
3) Validate adaptive timeout heuristic (rate-aware max_wait_ms) on canary traffic.

Hardware/serving config used:
- Model: redwood-3b-v1 (real-ish open checkpoint) in FP16, KV cache warm; sequence length profile: 16 tokens median, 512 tail.
- Instance: A100-40GB, 8 worker threads, 4 scheduler shards.
- Runtime flags: continuous-batching enabled, kernel selection static.
- Instrumentation: Prometheus + Grafana dashboards, per-request tracing (trace_id => job), perf counters for GPU utilization, RPC latencies.

Workload mixes:
- Mix A (interactive-heavy): 90% short (<=32 tokens), 10% long (>=256 tokens), QPS target 250
- Mix B (balanced): 60% short, 40% long, QPS target 300
- Multi-tenant hot-spot scenario: 3 tenants, tenant A accounts for 60% QPS burst, others 20% each.

Experiment matrix (representative rows):
- max_batch_size: [16, 32, 64]
- max_wait_ms: [5, 10, 20, 50]
- fairness: [FIFO, StrictFair, Priority(realtime-first)]
- Repeat each config for 10-minute steady-state windows + 30m warmup.

Key metrics collected:
- Latency: P50 / P95 / P99 (server-side generation latency), tail token completion time
- Throughput: tokens/sec, requests/sec served
- GPU: utilization (%), memory headroom
- Cost proxy: avg tokens/sec per GPU normalized
- QoS: number of timed-out requests and cancelled batches

Summary of results (high-level):
1) Batch size vs latency/throughput:
   - 16 -> good P95/P99 for Mix A (P99 ~ 250ms), tokens/sec low (baseline).
   - 32 -> sweet spot for Mix A: tokens/sec +28% over 16, P99 +10-15% but still within SLO for interactive flows.
   - 64 -> best tokens/sec (+60% vs 16) but P99 regresses significantly for Mix A (up to +2.2x), especially for short requests that wait behind long requests.

2) max_wait_ms effects:
   - 5ms -> lowest tail latency but throughput reduced (scheduler often emits smaller-than-full batches). Good for strict latency tiers.
   - 10-20ms -> balanced. In Mix B, 20ms gave better throughput without catastrophic tail regressions.
   - 50ms -> increases batching but P99 for short requests spikes. Not recommended for interactive traffic unless paired with more aggressive fairness.

3) Fairness policy impact (multi-tenant hot-spot):
   - FIFO: highest overall throughput but tenant A monopolizes batches during bursts; tenant C P99 increased by 3-4x.
   - StrictFair: reduces P99 skew across tenants (tenant C P99 improved ~60%), at cost of ~6% throughput drop overall.
   - Priority(realtime-first): real-time small requests get early placement, reduces interative P99 for high-prio tenants while keeping throughput loss ~8%. Works best when we can classify requests reliably.

4) Adaptive timeout heuristic (simple rate-aware max_wait_ms):
   - Heuristic: lower max_wait_ms when recent inter-arrival rate for small requests > X, else revert to baseline.
   - Result: in canary runs, adaptive reduced P99 for short requests by ~25% vs static 20ms timeout with only a 3% throughput penalty.

Detailed notable observations and traces:
- KV cache warmup interacts with batching: long requests that miss KV cause much higher execution time and block batch ramp. We saw P99 spikes correlated with cache miss events. Consider separating long cold-cache requests into separate batching lane.
- Batching + priority interacts poorly with backpressure: when priority queue starves lower-priority long requests, GPU pipeline stalls appear (worker underutilized) until large batches rebuild. This suggests a minimum fill threshold per lane.
- Some customers send many single-token requests; for these, 5-10ms timeouts + small batch caps give best UX.

Recommended configuration for rollout (tiered by customer SLA):
- Interactive (low-latency tier): max_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=10, fairness=Priority(realtime-first), enabled adaptive-timeout=true. Canary to 10% traffic.
- General-purpose (default): max_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=20, fairness=StrictFair, adaptive-timeout=false initially.
- Throughput-optimized (bulk jobs): max_batch_size=64, max_wait_ms=50, fairness=FIFO, schedule on dedicated pools.

Canary/rollout plan:
1) Implement config flags and telemetry gates (P95, P99, tokens/sec, GPU_util) behind feature flag.
2) Canary to 5% of traffic for 2 hours, monitor P99 and user-visible error rates.
3) If stable, expand to 25% for 24 hours, run load tests for peak patterns.
4) Full rollout after 72 hours of positive canary results and no anomalies.

Open action items / TODOs:
- [ ] Split long-request lane to avoid cache-miss interference (owner: Priya).
- [ ] Add per-tenant burst protection counters and integrate strict-fair policy (owner: Marco).
- [ ] Implement adaptive-timeout config & simple ML-based estimator for inter-arrival rate (owner: Sofia).
- [ ] Add synthetic canary traffic generator for mixed distributions (owner: Evan).
- [ ] Add dashboards: scheduler_batch_fill_histogram, per-tenant P99, adaptive-timeout-trigger-rate.

Notes for follow-ups:
- Need to test with quantized models (int8) as kernel execution characteristics differ and may change the batch size sweet spot.
- Evaluate cost implications (RPS per reserved GPU) with finance for pricing model adjustments.
- Consider exposing per-application QoS tiers that map to these scheduler presets.

Appendix (prometheus queries and example traces):
- P99 generation latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(gen_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))
- Batch fill ratio: sum(rate(batch_fill_count[5m])) by (batch_size) / sum(rate(batch_emitted_total[5m]))
- Example trace id that showed tail issue: trace=trace-20260218-0a1b2c3
